cards.q: How would you choose a polling interval?
cards.a: From how quickly a change must be visible and how many clients are polling. Ten clients polling a cheap endpoint every two seconds is fine; ten thousand clients doing it is a load problem. When the maths gets uncomfortable, that's the signal to move to push.

cards.t: Node 15 · Real time: polling and push
cards.q: How do you write a websocket message into the cache safely?
cards.a: setQueryData(key, old => ...) with an updater that compares versions or timestamps and returns old unchanged when the message is older than what's cached. Blind writes make out-of-order delivery a correctness bug.

cards.t: Node 15 · Real time: polling and push
cards.q: Why does the transport-independence of the cache matter architecturally?
cards.a: Because it means the decision between polling, SSE and websockets is an infrastructure decision you can revisit later without touching a single component. Very few architectural choices in a frontend are that cheaply reversible.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: What two performance wins does the query cache give you for free?
cards.a: Structural sharing — an unchanged refetch produces identical references and therefore no re-render. And deduplication — N components asking for one key make one request.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: What performance problem remains after those?
cards.a: A component that subscribes to a whole cache entry but needs one field of it. A header showing an unread count re-renders on every change to any notification.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: What does select do?
cards.a: Transforms a query's data before it reaches the component, and — crucially — compares the selected value, so the component only re-renders when that derived value actually changes.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: What is the trap with select?
cards.a: An inline select returning a new object or array on every call defeats the comparison entirely, because the result is never equal to the previous one. It must be a stable function returning a primitive or a memoised value.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: Which recurring pattern does the select trap belong to?
cards.a: Referential identity. It is the same problem as an inline object in a useEffect dependency array (Node 3) and an unstable query key object (Node 6), in its third costume.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: What is notifyOnChangeProps?
cards.a: A blunter subscription control: notifyOnChangeProps: ["data"] tells the query to only re-render the component when data changes, ignoring isFetching transitions entirely.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: What is a document cache?
cards.a: A cache where each key holds whatever the server returned, opaquely. TanStack Query and SWR work this way. If todo 42 appears in a list response and a detail response, those are two independent copies in two entries.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: What is a normalised cache?
cards.a: Responses are broken apart by type and ID into a flat store, so an entity exists exactly once and every query referencing it updates automatically when it changes. Apollo Client and urql work this way.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: Why does GraphQL make normalisation practical?
cards.a: Because the schema guarantees stable type and ID information on every object — that is what __typename and id conventions are for. Without reliable identity you cannot normalise.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: What is normalisation's cost?
cards.a: Complexity. It needs stable IDs on everything, explicit configuration for pagination and merge behaviour, and its failure modes (missing fields, cache misses, merge conflicts) are harder to reason about than a stale document.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: State TanStack Query's deliberate position on this.
cards.a: Invalidation is a simpler tool that reaches the same result at the cost of a round trip — and round trips are cheap while cache-consistency bugs are not. Being able to state that trade-off is a senior-sounding answer.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: What non-cache performance levers matter here?
cards.a: Have the server return only what the screen needs; virtualise long lists (TanStack Virtual, react-window) so ten thousand rows aren't ten thousand DOM nodes; and remember a well-indexed backend query beats any amount of client optimisation.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: How do you diagnose a re-render storm?
cards.a: React DevTools Profiler with “highlight updates” on, or the profiler's ranked view, to find which component re-renders and why. Then check whether it subscribes to more of a cache entry than it needs.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: What's the first thing to check when a page re-renders constantly?
cards.a: Whether components are subscribing to whole cache entries they only read a field of, and whether any query key or select produces a new reference each render. Referential instability is the cause far more often than the volume of data.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: How does normalisation handle pagination, and why is that its hard part?
cards.a: Paginated results are lists of references that must be merged into an existing list, and the cache can't know whether a new page appends, replaces or interleaves. That's why normalised clients need explicit merge functions per field — and why misconfiguring them produces duplicated or vanishing items.

cards.t: Node 16 · Performance and the normalisation question
cards.q: Is there a middle ground between document and normalised caches?
cards.a: Yes, in practice: a document cache plus disciplined key hierarchies and broad invalidation. You accept an extra round trip in exchange for never having to reason about merge semantics. That is TanStack Query's explicit bet.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: Describe the logout cache leak concretely.
cards.a: A user logs in on a shared machine, browses, and logs out. In an SPA the page never reloads, so the QueryClient is still in memory holding their data. The next user logs in, and their first render finds a warm cache showing someone else's information.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: What is the one-line fix?
cards.a: queryClient.clear() on logout — and defensively whenever a 401 forces a session to end.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: What is the second half of the fix?
cards.a: Put the identity in the key. ["profile"] is a bug; ["profile", userId] is not. The same applies to a tenant or organisation ID in a multi-tenant app.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: How does this follow from Node 6's rule?
cards.a: “Every input to the queryFn must be in the key” includes inputs that arrive implicitly — the user identity carried by a token or cookie is an input even though it never appears in your code.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: Compare bearer tokens and HttpOnly cookies for auth.
cards.a: A bearer token in an Authorization header is simple and immune to CSRF, but a token in JS-readable storage is readable by any XSS. An HttpOnly cookie can't be read by JavaScript at all, which is stronger against XSS, but it's sent automatically and therefore needs SameSite and CSRF protection.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: What does cookie auth require on the fetch and CORS side?
cards.a: credentials: "include" on the request, plus a server sending Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and a specific origin — the wildcard * is rejected with credentials, deliberately.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: What is the common production auth shape?
cards.a: A short-lived access token held in memory plus a long-lived refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie. The access token isn't persisted, so XSS can't steal a durable credential; the refresh token isn't readable by JavaScript at all.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: Describe the token refresh stampede.
cards.a: Five queries fire on page load and all five 401 at once, so all five kick off a token refresh. Four of them use a refresh token that rotation has already invalidated, and the user is logged out.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: What is the fix for the refresh stampede?
cards.a: A single shared in-flight refresh promise that every failing request awaits. Implement it once, in an Axios interceptor or a wrapped fetch — never inside individual queryFns.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: Where should auth headers be attached?
cards.a: In one wrapped fetch client or interceptor, not per query. Otherwise every new query is a chance to forget, and the refresh logic has nowhere to live.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: Why is this node a security topic, not a performance one?
cards.a: Because a shared process-wide cache with no notion of whose data it holds is a data leak. The failure mode isn't a slow page; it's showing one user another user's records.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: Why isn't “the user is redirected on logout” enough?
cards.a: In an SPA a redirect is a client-side route change, not a page load. The JavaScript context, and therefore the cache, is untouched. Only a full reload or an explicit clear() disposes of it.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: What should happen to the cache on a 401 mid-session?
cards.a: Treat it as a session end: clear the cache, stop in-flight refetches, and route to login. Leaving cached data on screen behind a login prompt is both confusing and a small disclosure risk on a shared device.

cards.t: Node 17 · Auth, tenancy, and cache safety
cards.q: Why does the wildcard CORS origin not work with credentials?
cards.a: Because Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * plus cookies would let any site on the internet make authenticated requests to your API and read the results. The spec rejects the combination, forcing the server to name the origin explicitly.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: What does cache persistence do?
cards.a: Writes the dehydrated cache to disk — via @tanstack/query-persist-client with a localStorage or IndexedDB persister — and restores it on boot, so a reload shows the last known data instantly and revalidates behind it.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: What are the three obligations of persisting a cache?
cards.a: (1) Never persist per-user data without clearing it on logout — that's Node 17's leak written to disk, surviving a browser restart. (2) Version it with a build-tied buster string, or a deploy that changes a data shape hydrates old objects into new code. (3) Respect maxAge, or you show three-week-old data as current.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: localStorage or IndexedDB for a persisted cache?
cards.a: localStorage is synchronous and roughly 5MB — fine for a small cache, but it blocks the main thread. IndexedDB is asynchronous and far larger, and is the right choice for anything substantial.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: What does networkMode control?
cards.a: How queries and mutations behave without a connection. The default "online" pauses queries rather than failing them, and queues mutations to fire when connectivity returns.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: What are the genuine hard problems of offline writes?
cards.a: Ordering (queued mutations must apply in a sensible sequence) and conflicts (the server's version has moved on while you were offline). Neither has a generic answer; both need domain decisions.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: Name the local-first ecosystem and what to know about it.
cards.a: Replicache, ElectricSQL, Yjs and CRDTs. [AWARE] — know they exist and know that “offline support” is a far larger commitment than adding a persister.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: When would you choose SWR over TanStack Query?
cards.a: A read-heavy app where you want a very small dependency and few knobs. Same core stale-while-revalidate model, but a much thinner mutation story and fewer features (no first-class infinite-query ergonomics of the same depth, lighter devtools).

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: When is RTK Query the right answer?
cards.a: When the codebase already uses Redux. It shares the store and devtools, and its endpoint-definition style with tag-based invalidation is a genuinely different and quite pleasant ergonomic — you declare which tags an endpoint provides and which a mutation invalidates.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: Apollo Client versus urql?
cards.a: Both GraphQL with normalised caches. Apollo is heavier, more featured, and more opinionated; urql is lighter and more composable, with normalisation as an opt-in exchange rather than the default.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: What is Relay and why is it rarely the right call?
cards.a: Facebook's GraphQL client — extremely powerful, with compile-time query optimisation and fragment colocation, but it requires a build compiler and strict schema conventions. The payoff needs a large org and a mature schema.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: Is fetch in a useEffect ever still the right answer?
cards.a: Yes — for a genuine one-off in a small app with no sharing, no staleness policy, and no writes. Being willing to say so is better than reflexively adding a data layer to a page with one request.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: What should decide your choice of data layer?
cards.a: Whether you're on GraphQL (normalised cache pays off), whether you already have Redux (RTK Query), how much interactivity there is (more interactivity → more value from a full cache), and bundle budget. Not fashion.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: What exactly gets persisted?
cards.a: The dehydrated query cache — keys, data, and metadata such as fetch times. Not the mutation cache by default, and not component state.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: What is a cache buster string, concretely?
cards.a: A version identifier — usually the build hash or app version — stored with the persisted cache and compared on restore. If it doesn't match, the persisted cache is discarded rather than hydrated into incompatible code.

cards.t: Node 18 · Persistence, offline, and the ecosystem
cards.q: Why is “offline support” a bigger commitment than it sounds?
cards.a: Reads are easy: persist and revalidate. Writes force you to answer ordering and conflict resolution, and to decide what the user sees when their queued change is finally rejected by the server. That's product design, not configuration.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: What does TanStack Query Devtools show you?
cards.a: Every cache key, its status (fresh, stale, fetching, inactive), its data, its observer count, and buttons to invalidate, refetch, or reset any entry. Half the confusion in this topic dissolves the first time you watch a key go stale on window blur.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: What does the browser network tab give you that devtools doesn't?
cards.a: The waterfall view (diagnoses Node 12), the initiator column (which code fired this), the actual request and response headers (diagnoses CORS and credentials), and throttling — which is how you make Node 4's race condition reproducible.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: Why is mocking fetch or stubbing your API module a weak testing strategy?
cards.a: It tests your mock. The request URL, method, headers, status handling, and error parsing all go untested, so the code most likely to be wrong is the code the test never exercises.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: What is Mock Service Worker (MSW) and why is it better?
cards.a: It intercepts at the network layer — a service worker in the browser, a request interceptor in Node — so your application makes a genuine fetch and MSW answers it. The URL, headers and status handling are all under test.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: What else does MSW unlock beyond unit tests?
cards.a: The same handlers serve component tests, integration tests, and local development against a backend that doesn't exist yet; and you can return a 500, a 429, or a two-second delay to exercise paths you'd otherwise never hit.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: Why must each test get its own QueryClient?
cards.a: Otherwise cached data and mutation state leak between tests, making them order-dependent and producing failures that vanish when run in isolation.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: Why set retry: false in tests?
cards.a: Because the default three retries with exponential backoff means a failure case takes several seconds of real waiting before your assertion can run — and often exceeds the test timeout.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: Why use findBy* rather than getBy* plus a sleep?
cards.a: findBy* returns a promise that retries until the element appears or times out, which is exactly right for async UI. A fixed sleep is either flaky (too short) or slow (too long) and is never correct.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: Which states do people forget to test?
cards.a: The error state, the empty state, and the second load — refetch-with-existing-data, where the isPending/isFetching distinction and keepPreviousData actually matter. Almost everyone tests only the happy first render.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: How do you test an optimistic update properly?
cards.a: Make MSW delay or fail the write. Assert that the UI changes before the response, then assert that it rolls back and shows an error on failure. Without a controllable delay, the optimistic window is too short to observe.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: What is left after this node?
cards.a: Nothing structural — this is the end of the chain. What remains is judgement, which comes from building the thing.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: How do you deliberately reproduce a race condition for testing?
cards.a: MSW with a per-request delay keyed on the parameter — make the first request slow and the second fast — then assert the UI shows the second subject's data. Without controllable timing, the bug is untestable.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: What does the devtools observer count tell you?
cards.a: How many mounted components are watching a key. A count of zero on data still on screen means you're rendering from a different key than you think; an unexpectedly high count often reveals accidental duplicate subscriptions.

cards.t: Node 19 · Seeing it and testing it
cards.q: What's the fastest way to confirm two components share one request?
cards.a: Devtools shows one entry with two observers, and the network tab shows one request. If you see two requests, the keys differ — usually an inline object, a Date, or a missing parameter.
